ButtonUnmaskSwap.label: Initial
fields: target_locations

Ordered list of world [x,y] locations of the containers associated with the cube colors requested in the instruction, in requested pickup order. Before covering, use the corresponding visible cube locations. At covering, associate each cube with the container descending over it. Subsequently follow that container continuously through every shuffle; its initial table slot is not its identity. Update to the last observed location each cycle, retaining a location through temporary arm occlusion. Track only requested targets, including the second target while manipulating the first. Do not assign an unseen color from the final arrangement alone. e.g. [[0.02, -0.18], [0.03, 0.13]]
tracking_frame

Label of the latest shown front frame in which all still-needed target containers, or their initially uncovered cubes, can be localized without arm occlusion. Retain the preceding value if no such frame appears in the cycle. This image anchors correspondence between the stored target locations and the next motion clip. Initialize with E0. e.g. "E114"
interaction_state

Observed interaction milestone, initially start. Button milestones are left_hover, left_ready, left_pressed, left_retracted, right_hover, right_ready, right_pressed, right_retracted, buttons_finished. Hover means the initial approach to that button has finished; ready means the subsequent short closing action has finished, even if the fingers were already closed on arrival. Pressed means the closed hand has descended into button contact; retracted means it has subsequently risen to approximately 0.15 m. buttons_finished means the hand has subsequently opened above the right button. Container milestones are target_hover, target_grasped, target_lifted, target_released, target_cleared. They respectively mean arrival at the selected container's 0.20 m approach, closure around it near 0.063 m, successful lift near 0.20 m, lowering and opening near 0.07 m, and empty-hand withdrawal near 0.15 m. Change only when the corresponding motion outcome is observed, never when its waypoint is selected. e.g. "right_ready"
pickups_completed

Number of requested containers successfully lifted in instruction order. Initialize to zero. Increment once when a newly grasped requested container is visibly raised off the table to approximately 0.20 m, exposing its cube. Do not increment for grasp closure, release, withdrawal, or repeated observations of the same lift. e.g. 1
target_locations

Read the requested colors in instruction order and initialize an ordered list of their visible cube world [x,y] locations using calibration. Match each descending cover to the cube underneath. Using the carried locations and tracking_frame, follow those specific containers through the cycle's chronological frames and write their latest [x,y] locations. Follow motion through exchanges rather than relabeling by nearest initial slot or final left-to-right order. Keep tracking a later requested target during button pressing and the earlier pickup. Preserve the last reliable location during temporary occlusion; use a newly exposed cube to confirm the association. e.g. [[0.02, -0.18], [0.03, 0.13]]
tracking_frame

Write the label of the latest frame shown this cycle in which all still-needed target containers, or initially uncovered target cubes, can be localized without arm occlusion. If none qualifies, carry the previous label. At the first cycle write E0. Use this retained image with target_locations to establish identities at the beginning of the next clip. e.g. "E114"
interaction_state

Initialize start. Update from observed outcomes and the incoming milestone, not from the action you are about to choose. A completed approach above the robot-left button gives left_hover; its subsequent short close-only motion gives left_ready; descent to button contact gives left_pressed; upward withdrawal gives left_retracted. Apply the analogous right_hover, right_ready, right_pressed, right_retracted milestones at the robot-right button. In particular, arrival with already-closed fingers is still right_hover, not right_ready: the separate short closing action must be observed. Opening after right_retracted gives buttons_finished. Arrival above the next requested container at about 0.20 m gives target_hover; descending and closing around it near 0.063 m gives target_grasped; lifting it clear near 0.20 m gives target_lifted; lowering and opening near 0.07 m gives target_released; withdrawing the empty hand near 0.15 m gives target_cleared. A subsequent approach to the next target returns to target_hover. Retain the incoming state if the expected outcome has not occurred or no control steps executed. e.g. "right_ready"
pickups_completed

Initialize zero. Increment only when the incoming state is target_grasped and the current clip shows the held requested container successfully raised clear to about 0.20 m, ordinarily revealing its colored cube. Carry the count unchanged in every other situation, including further views of that same held container. e.g. 1
inst.subgoal:
Use the incoming memory together with outcomes visible this cycle to determine the current milestone; write those observations for the next cycle. Begin by locating both buttons and all requested colored cubes. Robot-left is larger world y, appearing on the right of the front image. Estimate geometry with the calibrated cameras, intersecting image rays with the appropriate object surface height rather than treating elevated tops as table points. Use wrist imagery to refine alignment. Do not reuse episode-specific coordinates.

Button rules: From start, approach the robot-left button center at z=0.15 m, orientation [-3.1416,0,0], gripper open. At left_hover, command closure above the same center at z=0.15. At left_ready, descend over that center to commanded z=0.0075, closed. Actual contact may stop the TCP near z=0.024; this counts as contact, not a reason to press deeper. At left_pressed, retract to z=0.15 closed. At left_retracted, approach the robot-right button center at z=0.15 with an open command. At right_hover, perform the separate short closing action above the button even when the reported fingers are already closed. At right_ready, descend to z=0.0075 closed. At right_pressed, retract to z=0.15 closed. At right_retracted, open above the same button. Continue observing and tracking container exchanges throughout all these motions. Neither a return to the original spatial arrangement nor an unchanged shell appearance resets its hidden color association.

Container rules: After buttons_finished, select target_locations[pickups_completed]. At target_cleared, select that same indexed next uncompleted target. Approach its current center at z=0.20, open, pointing straight down. Choose yaw from its visible square edges so the fingers grasp opposing sides; use an equivalent square-symmetry orientation near zero where possible. At target_hover, descend to the container center at z=0.0633–0.0634 and close. At target_grasped, raise to z=0.20 closed, keeping the grasp orientation and approximately the container center's x,y; a small visual centering correction is appropriate. Fingers stopped around 0.018 m each and a container between them support a successful grasp.

At target_lifted, if more requested pickups remain, lower the held container over its current location to z=0.07 and open, preserving current orientation. At target_released, withdraw vertically with open fingers to approximately z=0.149 before moving laterally to the next target. The completed pickup remains completed even though its cube is covered again. After lifting the final requested container, retain the grasp for automatic success; do not initiate an unnecessary release.

Never issue an exactly identical TCP pose merely to change the gripper. If the nominal close/open waypoint is within 2 mm of the current pose, add a small vertical displacement of about 3 mm while retaining the required gripper command. Allow normal motion error when recognizing arrival; do not require exact equality.

If an expected motion did not execute, retain memory milestones and retry with a reachable, nonidentical waypoint. If alignment or grasp is visibly unsuccessful, correct using the current wrist image instead of advancing progress. If a target is temporarily occluded, first withdraw safely to reveal it. If containers are still moving and correspondence needs another observation, a short purposeful wait of 8 control steps may be used to finish tracking before a grasp. Do not guess a hidden color from its original slot, and do not wait without a specific visibility or settling purpose.

Ordered list of central-axis world [x,y] coordinates of the containers associated with the requested cube colors, in fixed requested pickup order. Before covering, use the central axes of the corresponding visible cubes. At covering, associate each cube with the container descending over it. Localize a resting container using its horizontal top-face center projected at approximately z=0.06 m, not its silhouette centroid or a table-plane projection of its elevated top. For a lifted container, account for its observed elevation. Follow each container continuously through every shuffle, allowing its horizontal and vertical image ranking to change at crossings; neither its initial slot nor nearest position alone establishes identity. Check correspondence through successive frames across the episode and correct an erroneous association at its first occurrence and throughout its subsequent values, rather than switching identities at the endpoint. Update coordinates after observed translation, including movement during grasping or release. Preserve the carried coordinate when stationary and retain the last reliable estimate through temporary occlusion. Write coordinates to millimetre resolution without implying millimetre measurement accuracy. Track only requested targets, including the second target while manipulating the first. highlight_frame

lifted_count

inst.subgoal:
Start with an open hand and approach the button. Interpret all positions in world coordinates using the supplied camera calibration; estimate button and cube locations from their geometry, not raw image left/right. Use the wrist view to refine alignment. Recover target identities from highlight_frame after their white areas disappear, matching by position as well as color; never select every cube of a highlighted color. Use the observations of this cycle together with carried memory to recognize newly completed presses and lifts before selecting the action.

Button rules: If button_pressed is false and the hand is not yet above the button, move to its center at z=0.15, roll=-3.1416, pitch=0, yaw=0, gripper open. If above the button at approach height with open fingers, close at the same nominal approach waypoint. If above it with closed fingers and no observed contact yet, descend to its center at z=0.0075 with fingers closed. Once contact is observed, retract to the button center at z=0.15, keeping closed; do not repeat the press merely because the actual contact height is higher than the command. After retracting, open at the button approach waypoint before traveling to a cube.

Pickup rules: Order highlighted targets red, green, blue, with same-color ties by increasing world x then y. Select the first target not already represented by lifted_count. With open fingers and adequate table clearance, approach its center at z=0.15. Use roll=3.1416, pitch=0 and a yaw aligned to its horizontal square edges, choosing the equivalent square orientation in approximately [-0.7854,0.7854]. Once above that target, descend to its center at z=0.02 and close. Allow normal approach error of roughly 1–1.5 cm rather than repeatedly commanding the hover. With the cube grasped at low height, lift vertically to z=0.15 with fingers closed, preserving the aligned yaw. Estimate its grasp center from the visible cube and wrist geometry rather than treating a small TCP tracking error as a new target location.

Handling additional targets: Once a pickup lift is visibly complete, it counts even if the cube is subsequently returned. If another highlighted target remains and a counted cube is still held at hover height, lower at the current TCP x,y to z=0.01, retaining current orientation, and open on arrival. If the hand is low and open over that returned cube, retract vertically to approximately z=0.15 with fingers open before moving laterally. When retracted, approach the next uncounted target, not the cube just returned. After lifting the final target, keep it held; success should end the episode without requiring a placement.

Every gripper-only change must include at least 2 mm of translation if its nominal waypoint would otherwise equal the reported TCP pose; use a small upward adjustment, within 5 mm. Do not advance memory on an action that executed no steps. If alignment or grasp evidence is ambiguous, use the current wrist image to correct the relevant object-centered approach at safe height; a failed empty grasp should be retried without counting it. If no target evidence has yet been captured after the button operation, use a short bounded wait specifically to observe the highlight display and inspect every returned frame. Do not invent targets or repeatedly press a confirmed button. For an otherwise unmatched situation, preserve known task facts, keep a visibly held cube closed, and retract vertically to safe clearance before reassessing.

If the open hand at hover is already aligned within roughly 1–1.5 cm above an uncompleted highlighted cube, select that cube and descend rather than redirecting to another target. Back-project two endpoints of a cube top-face edge onto the same top-face height plane using the calibrated ray-plane intersection. fields: target_location

The world xy location of the demonstrated block at the END of the demonstration, stored as [x,y]. Identify the block actually lifted, then track its physical identity continuously through all subsequent exchanges of positions; do not retain its original slot. At the video cycle write its final location. During execution retain this location unless the same block is visibly released at a displaced location, in which case update to its new resting xy. This identifies the rightmost red block in episode 70, the leftmost green block in 76 and 56, the leftmost red block in 6, and the demonstrated foreground red block in 95. Infer coordinates using calibration and the block's tabletop geometry, not image left/right as world axes. e.g. [0.014, 0.160]
completed_repetitions

Number of execution pick-up-and-put-down repetitions completed, excluding the demonstration. Initialize to zero at the video cycle. Increment at the first act cycle showing the lifted target returned to the table and released with open fingers. Thus the release cycles, not the outgoing release commands or subsequent empty-hand retreats, change this value. Retain it on all other cycles, including zero-step cycles and button actions. e.g. 1
target_location

At the video cycle identify the block that the hand lifts. Follow that physical block through the remaining video, including every exchange with an indistinguishable block, and write its final world xy as [x,y]. Use calibrated tabletop geometry to localize it. Never select simply the slot originally grasped: exchanges can change which slot contains the target. During execution carry this location forward; when the observed motion shows the target released at a displaced resting location, update its xy using the visible block and hand geometry. While it is held or occluded retain the previous resting location. e.g. [0.014, 0.160]
completed_repetitions

Initialize to zero in the video cycle. Increment once when this cycle's motion shows the held, raised target descending to the tabletop and the current fingers open to release it. Do not increment merely for closing, lifting, choosing a release waypoint, or lifting the empty hand away. Preserve the count during other motions, button operations, and explicitly zero-step cycles. The demonstration never counts. e.g. 1
inst.subgoal:
At the video cycle output memory only. Read the required execution repetition count N from the goal: 'again' means one, 'two times' means two, and 'three times' means three. Use target_location to identify the correct physical block in the execution scene, not the block's original demonstration slot. Apply memory updates from observed events before deciding whether more repetitions are needed.

Localize tabletop objects with the calibrated front and wrist cameras. Estimate a cube's center and edge direction in world coordinates using its visible top surface at approximately z=0.04 m; grasp TCP height is 0.02 m. Use a downward hand, roll pi (equivalently -pi), pitch zero, with yaw aligned to the cube edges modulo pi/2. Do not hard-code an episode's xy or yaw. Heights below are world metres.

When execution starts with the hand high and open, move above the target center at z=0.15, keeping it open. If fewer than N repetitions are complete and the open hand has just approached or realigned above the target, descend to its center at z=0.02 and close. The actual reported approach pose can differ from the intended center by about a centimetre; use visual localization rather than treating that error as a new task stage.

If the hand is low and closed around the target, lift to z=0.15 with the same grasp alignment, keeping it closed. Keep xy nearly fixed, correcting only a few millimetres toward the centered grasp if needed. If the target is held at the raised height, lower at the current TCP xy to z=0.01, preserving orientation, and open at arrival. This is the put-down action, regardless of how many repetitions have already completed.

When the hand is open and low after release, retreat vertically to approximately z=0.15, keeping it open and preserving orientation. Do this even after the final repetition; do not move laterally to the button while still low. If the observed motion is this empty-hand retreat and completed_repetitions is less than N, first issue an open-hand realignment above the newly localized target center at z=0.15 with its current edge-aligned yaw. On the cycle after that realignment, descend and close for the next repetition. Distinguish retreat from realignment using this cycle's motion frames, not an assumed unseen action history.

If completed_repetitions equals N and the released target is on the table with the open hand raised clear, move above the circular stop button at z=0.15, roll=-pi, pitch=0, yaw=0, keeping the gripper open. Localize the button's center, not the center of a neighboring cube. When above the button with open fingers, close the empty gripper while commanding the centered z=0.15 pose. Ensure at least 2 mm displacement from the reported TCP; if necessary use a 5 mm upward offset. When above the button with closed fingers, descend to the button center at commanded z=0.0075, keeping closed. Contact may stop the actual TCP around z=0.0245; this is not a reason to repeatedly push deeper. When the current motion shows that downward button contact and the closed hand is low over the button, retract to z=0.15, still closed.

For an unanticipated misalignment or failed grasp, use visible geometry to recover: raise clear with an empty open hand, recenter over the remembered target, and retry without increasing the repetition count. Never substitute another block or count a failed lift. Avoid identical-pose commands, unsafe lateral movement at tabletop height, and purposeless waits. If localization is temporarily obscured, retreat vertically to reveal the target rather than guessing a new identity.

VideoPlaceButton.label: Initial
fields: post_button_target

At the video cycle, record the earliest shown frame in which the instructed cube has been released onto the first target it is placed on after the button press, with the hand lifted enough to distinguish the released cube from a held cube. Ignore the target occupied before the press and the later off-target reset placement. Carry this frame label unchanged through all act cycles. For the supplied episodes the labels are respectively V448, V480, V448, V512, and V432. e.g. "V448"
post_button_target

During the video cycle, locate the hand's downward press on the gray button on its white base. Follow the instructed-color cube after that press to its next target placement. Save the earliest shown frame where it has been released there and the hand has lifted enough to distinguish release from continued holding. Do not select its pre-press target or its subsequent off-target reset position. At every act cycle copy the incoming label unchanged. e.g. "V448"
inst.subgoal:
At the video cycle output memory only. Execution begins with an open hand above the table and the instructed-color cube at its reset position. The instruction refers to a temporal relationship in the demonstration: place the cube on the target used immediately after the demonstrated button press. Do not press the button in execution, replay the earlier placement, or wait for a new button event.

Use post_button_target to identify the purple ring underneath the released instructed-color cube in the saved demonstration frame. Match that ring to the current scene using the stationary ring layout and button. This is the destination, even if another ring is closer to the cube. Ignore cubes of other colors.

Estimate world positions using calibrated camera rays. Intersect ring-center rays with the tabletop plane z=0. Estimate cube horizontal center using its top face at approximately z=0.04 rather than projecting its image center onto the table. Use the current wrist view to refine alignment. Orient the hand straight down, roll approximately pi and pitch zero, with yaw aligned to the cube's horizontal edges; maintain that orientation while carrying and releasing it.

Apply these observable-state rules: If the hand is open, the cube is not already on the remembered destination, and the hand is not at its pickup approach, move above the cube center to z=0.15 with gripper open. If the open hand is at this approach (allowing normal endpoint error), descend to the cube center at z=0.02 and close. If the cube is grasped and the hand is low at pickup, lift vertically to z=0.15 with gripper closed. If holding the cube at clearance height but not above the destination, move horizontally to the destination center at z=0.15 with gripper closed. If holding the cube above the destination at clearance height, descend at that destination center to commanded z=0.005 and open. If the hand is open and low over the cube released onto the destination, retract vertically to z=0.15 with gripper open. Do not mistake a recently released cube for a fresh pickup; its position on the remembered destination and the open fingers establish the retreat condition. Do not insist that the measured release height equal 0.005: contact can leave the TCP around 0.01–0.02.

Use approximate arrival tolerances of 0.02 m at approach height and 0.01 m horizontally above the destination, refining the actual destination from the visible ring rather than substituting the imperfect reached TCP position. Preserve closed fingers throughout lift and transport. Never issue an identical-pose waypoint merely to change the gripper; include at least 0.002 m of movement.

For an unrecognized or ambiguous state, use the visible grasp and geometry to recover: lift a securely held cube to clearance before lateral movement; with an empty hand, move open to a clear elevated observation pose and relocalize the instructed cube and remembered ring. Do not choose a different target because the intended one is occluded. If the cube is already correctly placed, withdraw without disturbing it.

MoveCube.label: Initial
fields: method

At the video cycle classify the demonstrated means of moving the cube: 'hand_push' when the closed empty hand slides the cube along the table, 'tool_push' when the robot first grasps the long bar and uses it to slide the cube, or 'pick_place' when it grasps and lifts the cube before transporting it. Keep this value throughout execution. Classify by actual object motion, not by whether the hand temporarily occludes the cube. e.g. "tool_push"
initial_scene

At the video cycle write 'unknown'. At the first execution cycle write the label of its current frame, preserving the execution's initial cube position, cube orientation, target position, and bar geometry as one scene keyframe. Retain that label for the rest of execution, including when these features become occluded or move. e.g. "E0"
method

When shown the demonstration, write 'hand_push' if the empty closed hand slides the cube on the table, 'tool_push' if the robot picks up the long bar and pushes the cube with it, or 'pick_place' if the cube is grasped, raised, transported, and released. Distinguish pushing from grasping by whether the cube rises with the hand, not by occlusion. On execution cycles copy the carried value unchanged. e.g. "tool_push"
initial_scene

During the video cycle write 'unknown'. On the first execution cycle, when this field is 'unknown', write the current execution frame label. Otherwise copy the carried label unchanged. Use the retained scene rather than substituting the demonstration's object locations. e.g. "E0"
inst.subgoal:
On a video cycle output memory only. Execution starts with the open hand high above the table. Select the manipulation family from method; do not copy demonstration world positions. Use the initial execution scene, or the current scene when initial_scene is still unknown, to establish the original cube center C, target center T, cube yaw, and bar endpoints. Recover world coordinates using calibrated image rays and the table plane; account for cube height when locating its center rather than projecting the center of its visible silhouette onto the table. Use the wrist view to refine estimates. All distances below are metres. Let d=(T-C)/|T-C| in the horizontal plane. Use downward orientation, roll pi or -pi and pitch zero. Test arrival with tolerances appropriate to the reported pose, allowing approximately 0.015 horizontal error after a long approach; do not repeatedly reissue an approach just because the robot undershot it.

For hand_push: the initial waypoint is behind the cube at C-0.05d, z=0.02, closing the gripper at arrival. Set yaw along the push line modulo pi, choosing the equivalent angle closest to zero. This is a push with an empty closed gripper, not a cube grasp. When the closed hand is low behind the cube and the cube has not yet reached the target, move directly along the table to T-0.02d, z=0.02, keeping the gripper closed and preserving yaw. When that endpoint has been reached and the cube is on the target, open at the same nominal endpoint. Do not insert a lift or an intermediate overhead approach in this family.

For pick_place: with an open hand not yet over the cube, approach the original cube center at z=0.15, open, yaw aligned to a cube edge using the equivalent grasp orientation nearest zero. With the open hand above the cube, descend to C at z=0.02 and close. A low closed hand holding the cube near its original location must lift vertically to z=0.15; it must not immediately travel low toward the target. Use the retained cube center for this lift, refined by any small observed cube displacement during grasping. A raised closed hand holding the cube away from the target moves to T at z=0.15, closed, preserving its current orientation. A raised closed hand already over T descends to T at z=0.005 and opens at arrival. A low open hand at T after release retracts vertically to z=0.15, open. The visible held cube and finger separation distinguish a grasp from the empty closed hand used in pushing. Use current position relative to C and T, object attachment, and the motion frames to distinguish lifting at the source from lowering at the destination.

For tool_push: grasp near one end of the bar, leaving most of its length projecting from the hand. Choose the end nearer the robot, with the grasp center about 0.02 inward from that end. Initially approach this grasp center at z=0.20 with the gripper open and yaw along the bar's long axis modulo pi. When open above that grasp point, descend to z=0.01 and close. When closed low holding the bar at its original location, lift to z=0.20 at the same horizontal grasp point. When the bar is raised, move to the push-start pose at z=0.02, closed. For this pose orient the bar perpendicular to d. Choose a unit vector n perpendicular to d such that the bar extends from the grasp toward the cube, respecting the end that was grasped. The intended contact region is about 0.10 along the bar from the grasp. Put the TCP at C-0.10d-0.10n and choose yaw so the held bar actually points along n; account for its fixed attachment to the hand. This puts the bar behind the cube with clearance before the pushing stroke. When the held bar is low at this staging position, move straight along d to T-0.03d-0.10n, z=0.02, closed, without changing orientation. When the cube is on the target and the stroke endpoint has been reached, open at that endpoint. Do not mistake the raised bar at its original grasp location for completion of the push.

For any release that would otherwise command an identical current pose, retain the nominal endpoint if it differs by at least 0.002; otherwise add a 0.003 upward displacement while opening. Do not add a substantial retreat before release. Never use finger closure alone as evidence that the cube was grasped: inspect object attachment and method. If a situation is not covered, use current images and the retained initial scene to recover the closest unmet geometric condition for the selected family. If localization is temporarily impossible, use a short wait to obtain another observation rather than inventing coordinates or switching methods. If an action executed no steps, do not infer progress.

At a video cycle output memory only. Execution starts with the open hand above the scene. Read demonstration to identify the peg actually lifted, the particular colored end between the fingers, and the box face entered by the other end. Track the selected peg backward to its initial position; do not select by color alone, since multiple pegs can share colors. Distinguish grasping an end from inserting that end: the free end enters the box. The selected box face can be on either image side. Robot left is +y, which appears on the right of the front image.

Use calibrated image geometry rather than copying episode-specific world coordinates. Recover tabletop peg axes and endpoints by intersecting camera rays with their appropriate height planes. With world-to-camera extrinsics [R|t], use camera center C = -R^T t and world ray direction d = R^T K^-1[u,v,1]^T. For a landmark at height h, compute lambda = (h - C_z)/d_z and X = C + lambda d before measuring world distances. Use the landmark's height, not automatically the tabletop height. Distinguish visible top-surface landmarks, the peg centerline, inner finger surfaces, and the TCP between the fingertips. Intersect a visible surface pixel at that surface's height, not at centerline height; recover the centerline and opposing-contact midpoint using the fitted peg cross-section and finger geometry. A visible finger edge is not the contact midpoint. When contact is hidden, constrain it with both opposing fingers and the rigid peg across neighboring demonstration frames rather than substituting an exposed colored point. Retain numerical precision through fitting and waypoint output; do not round coordinates to centimetres. Fit the box footprint and orientation from its edges. Use the wrist image to refine visible geometry. Use its supplied camera extrinsics and the reported TCP pose to recover visible held-peg landmarks in hand-relative coordinates; do not assume the wrist-image center is the TCP. At open-hand approach, use the wrist view to refine current peg landmarks without redefining the demonstrated contact as the reached TCP. Determine peg identity, grasped end, and contact position separately. Fit the whole peg and the opposing fingertip contacts together across closing and early lifting demonstration frames. Track both colored segments, their boundary, and the contact region back to the unobstructed initial peg. The grasped segment is the one enclosed by the fingers; neither prominence nor visibility in the wrist image establishes whether a segment is held or free. Track both ends through lift and transport and check which remains free during insertion to confirm the grasped end. Define a directed unit peg axis a from the held end toward the free end and locate the color boundary b. Fit the midpoint c of opposing fingertip contacts jointly with the peg endpoints and boundary; recover its signed longitudinal offset s = (c - b) dot a, rather than assuming contact at a segment center. Fit the directed axis from full peg edges and endpoints in calibrated world geometry, not from the front-image line angle. Check the contact's distance from both the boundary and the held endpoint, and require the same longitudinal contact to explain the opposing fingers across closure and early lift. Before choosing the approach or closing descent, reconstruct the current boundary and axis at peg height and map the demonstrated contact to b_current + s a_current in the tabletop plane. Refit these landmarks in the elevated open-hand view even when the resulting descent corrects more than a centimetre of approach tracking error. Do not substitute the peg midpoint, segment midpoint, or reached TCP for this contact. At pickup use a downward hand, roll approximately -pi and pitch approximately zero, align the hand's longitudinal axis with the peg, and close across its width; choose the yaw equivalent that matches the demonstration. For later manipulation, reconstruct the demonstrated orientation rather than imposing zero pitch.

Apply the following rules according to the observed pose, held object, and motion frames, not according to cycle number. If the hand is empty and not yet above the demonstrated grasp location, move open to that location at z=0.20 m with the pickup yaw. If it is open above that location near z=0.20 m, descend to the same nominal x,y at z=0.01 m and close. Recompute the nominal contact location from the visible peg geometry at the elevated open-hand configuration, not from the reached TCP. Use this same nominal x,y for the open approach, closing descent, and pickup lift. A reached approach displaced by more than a centimetre does not imply that the intended approach and contact locations differ. If the fingers have closed around the selected peg near table height, lift closed to z=0.20 m at that same nominal location and yaw.

If the selected peg has been lifted but has not yet been transported to the insertion approach, move closed to the demonstrated elevated transport endpoint. Separate endpoint selection from pose fitting. First identify the transition from completed lateral relocation and rotation to descent, then independently identify the transition from descent to inward movement for low staging. Fit each transition's contact pose using adjacent frames; an earlier sample during relocation is not the completed transport endpoint. Enforce one rigid peg-to-hand relationship across these fits unless visible evidence shows slip. Fit transport height and orientation independently of pickup; do not inherit pickup's z=0.20 m or exactly downward orientation. Fit each pose relative to the entered box face using neighboring demonstration frames, visible peg edges and endpoints, color boundary, and the midpoint between opposing fingertip contacts. Recover the rigid peg-to-TCP offset and constrain the actual held-peg offset with the current wrist image. Fit candidate hand rotation R_hand and TCP translation jointly by reprojecting the rigid peg and contact landmarks into the calibrated demonstration views: each landmark has world position p_TCP + R_hand r, where r is its fitted hand-relative offset. Compare projected endpoints, color boundary, peg edges, and opposing finger contacts with the observed geometry, using neighboring frames to resolve occlusion and the end of motion. Enforce p_TCP = p_landmark - R_hand r consistently across visible landmarks. Constrain rotation with both the directed held-to-free axis and finger-contact arrangement, not an unsigned image line angle. Accept transport and staging estimates only after checking their landmark reprojections; neither arbitrary face clearance nor the image boundary locates a clipped TCP. Use these same contact constraints to reconstruct low staging independently, without rounding coordinates or lowering from the measured transport endpoint. If the hand is partly outside the image, infer its position from the visible held peg and demonstrated grasp offset, not an arbitrary clearance beyond the face. Project elevated geometry at its elevated height, not onto the tabletop. The TCP is neither the free tip nor the opening center. Resolve yaw's pi ambiguity using the directed held-to-free-end vector together with the demonstrated peg-to-hand contact relationship; do not assume that the positive hand axis points toward the free tip. Preserve demonstrated non-cardinal orientations. Reproduce demonstrated transport tilt and height; approximately 0.19 m is only an initial estimate for nearly level transport, not a universal target. Do not assume the transport endpoint lies directly above low staging, and do not move directly from pickup into the opening.

If the hand is at the elevated transport endpoint, move closed to the independently reconstructed low staging pose immediately before inward entry. Compute its intended box-relative position rather than preserving the measured transport endpoint. Ordinary transport tracking error is not evidence of a demonstrated inward translation during descent; include such translation only when the demonstrated geometry supports it. Reconstruct height and pitch together so the free tip approaches the opening correctly. For nearly level staging, TCP height near 0.04 m is an initial estimate, not an invariant; preserve demonstrated lower or tilted staging when present. If the hand is at completed low staging, target the endpoint of the demonstrated first inward alignment advance, not an arbitrary sampled image along that advance. For the nearly level entry pattern, this advance is approximately 0.05 m along the inward face normal, with demonstrated lateral and height corrections. Compute it from the reconstructed nominal staging pose rather than simply adding displacement to the reached TCP. Entry may instead combine inward translation with substantial height and pitch correction when supported by the demonstration. Align the free tip with the opening, not the TCP, and keep the gripper closed.

After an inward advance, compare the current motion frames and peg-to-opening relationship with the demonstrated motion segments. Video frames sample motion; they are not a list of commanded waypoints. Identify completed staging, the endpoint of the first inward alignment advance, and terminal insertion from neighboring frames and changes in translation, height, or orientation. Require evidence of a distinct completed intermediate maneuver before selecting another intermediate target; an intervening sampled pose or a still-exposed free tip alone is not such evidence. Once the first alignment advance has completed, target terminal insertion unless a distinct further alignment maneuver is supported. Preserve any such demonstrated maneuver, including tilted-entry corrections, rather than skipping it. Reconstruct target geometry without a universal advance length or 0.05 m cap. Through an otherwise straight insertion advance, preserve the established insertion-axis orientation; change it only when peg-axis and fingertip-contact geometry support the change, not merely because the projected arm or wrist silhouette changes. When terminal insertion is the next appropriate configuration, reconstruct the entered face plane and the demonstrated opposing fingertip-contact midpoint in the final demonstration frames. Express that contact relative to the face as separate inward-normal distance, lateral alignment, and height. Map this face-relative geometry to the current box and recover the TCP using the fitted grasp offset. Check the inferred TCP standoff against the remaining exposed peg length and contact geometry. Map the proposed terminal target back into the demonstration's box-relative frame and reproject its fitted hand and peg landmarks into the final demonstration view. Compare the predicted opposing fingertip-contact landmarks with the demonstrated fingers, and the predicted exposed peg between contact and entered face with the visible exposed length. Reject a depth fit that places contact farther inward than the demonstrated fingers, even if its free tip would lie securely inside the box. Check inward-normal distance, lateral alignment, and height separately; free-tip alignment alone does not validate terminal depth. Do not advance until the TCP approaches the face, place it at the opening, infer depth from the free tip alone, or impose a fixed remaining travel distance. This terminal-depth fit applies only when terminal insertion is the next supported target; it does not establish an otherwise unobserved intermediate stopping point. Keep the gripper closed through the demonstrated pickup lift, transport, staging, and insertion motions. A red indicator confirms successful insertion but specifies neither an additional waypoint nor a gripper command. Apply any separately supplied post-success action convention; do not extrapolate an unseen continuation from the terminal demonstration image.

Use the current motion frames to distinguish a completed lift from completed transport and a completed descent from completed horizontal insertion. Compare the current configuration to the retained demonstration when the current wrist view shows only the held peg or table; do not interpret an occluded box as a missing box. Allow approximately centimetre-scale tracking error when recognizing a completed long move, but compute the next waypoint from the intended geometry.

For an unlisted or uncertain configuration, localize the held peg, box, and closest demonstrated configuration again. If holding the peg with uncertain clearance, lift vertically to safe clearance before correcting alignment; if empty, approach the demonstrated peg open. Never insert blindly when the free tip is visibly misaligned. Use a small corrective waypoint when necessary, and never issue an identical TCP waypoint merely to change the gripper. No purposeless waiting is required.

PatternLock.label: Initial
fields: pattern

An ordered list of grid nodes visited in the demonstration, including the starting node and every subsequent segment endpoint. Represent each node as [row,column], with zero-based rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right in the front image. At the video cycle, extract the entire ordered path from stick motion, newly red endpoints, and connecting traces. Repeated frames of one visit add nothing; a genuine return to a node adds another occurrence. Preserve intermediate visited endpoints even when successive segments are collinear. Carry this list unchanged through execution. e.g. [[2,1],[2,2],[1,2],[0,1]]
reached_index

Zero-based index in pattern of the latest consecutively reached demonstration endpoint during execution. Write 0 at the video cycle and at the initial execution cycle, where the stick already occupies the demonstrated starting node. At subsequent cycles, advance only when the observed execution has reached the next listed node, as established by the stick location and endpoint activation; accept positioning error within 1 cm. Record observed arrival, not the destination of the waypoint being chosen at this cycle. Otherwise retain the previous value. e.g. 1
pattern

At the video cycle, identify the stationary marker grid and write the complete ordered list of demonstrated visited nodes, including the initial red node. Encode nodes as [row,column], using zero-based rows top to bottom and columns left to right in the front image. Follow the stick and changes in red endpoints and connecting traces chronologically. Do not add duplicates for repeated frames at one endpoint; do include genuine revisits and intermediate visited endpoints along collinear segments. During every act cycle copy the incoming list unchanged. e.g. [[2,1],[2,2],[1,2],[0,1]]
reached_index

Write 0 during the video cycle and at execution step zero: the stick starts on pattern[0]. At later act cycles, inspect the current pose and the motion frames for arrival at pattern[incoming reached_index + 1]. If the stick has reached that node within 1 cm and the visible endpoint activation supports arrival, increment by one; otherwise retain the incoming value. Never increment merely because you are about to command a move. If no steps executed, retain the value. e.g. 1
inst.subgoal:
During the video cycle write memory only. Execution starts with the stick already at the first demonstrated node; do not command that starting pose again. Identify the square marker grid from the current front image, using the wrist image to resolve occlusion. Its spacing is 0.10 m and its center is (x,y)=(-0.10,0). For an N-by-N grid, node [r,c] has x=-0.10+0.10*(r-(N-1)/2) and y=0.10*(c-(N-1)/2). Thus upward in the front image means decreasing world x, and rightward means increasing world y. Count actual grid rows and columns, not just currently unobscured markers. Use calibration and visible markers to check this registration.

Determine the latest reached index using the incoming reached_index and observed arrival at its next node, applying the memory update rule. If another node remains, command exactly that next node's world x and y, z=0.070 m, retaining the current approximately downward TCP orientation. Keep the gripper closed (command -1; the stick interface ignores it). Move directly between successive demonstrated endpoints, including diagonals, without lifting, adding intermediate waypoints, or pausing to reproduce demonstration timing. Target the ideal grid coordinates rather than adding an offset to the imperfect current TCP pose. Arrival within 1 cm is sufficient to move on; do not unnecessarily correct the few-millimetre residual errors shown after motions.

If the next endpoint has not been reached, target that same endpoint rather than skipping it. If a motion executed no steps, do not advance progress; re-estimate the endpoint from the available images and retry a reachable, nonidentical waypoint toward it. If registration is uncertain, fit the regular 0.10 m grid to visible markers using calibration and the known current stick node, then use the best-supported next endpoint from pattern; do not invent a different pattern. Once the final endpoint is visibly reached, make no additional tracing motion; if another response is required before automatic termination, wait a single control step to allow success evaluation.

Represent each node as [row,column], with zero-based rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right in the front image. At the video cycle, extract the entire ordered path from stick motion, newly red endpoints, and connecting traces. Repeated frames of one visit add nothing; a genuine return to a node adds another occurrence. Preserve intermediate visited endpoints even when successive segments are collinear. Carry this list unchanged through execution. e.g. [[2,1],[2,2],[1,2],[0,1]]
reached_index

Zero-based index in pattern of the latest consecutively reached demonstration endpoint during execution. Write 0 at the video cycle and at the initial execution cycle, where the stick already occupies the demonstrated starting node. At subsequent cycles, scan the observed motion chronologically, starting from the carried index. Advance through every consecutive listed endpoint whose arrival is established by stick position within 1 cm and supporting endpoint activation; do not limit advancement to one endpoint per cycle. Record only confirmed arrival, not the destination being commanded or an action-only near-arrival allowance. Proximity outside 1 cm does not advance this field. Otherwise retain the previous value. If no steps execute, retain the previous value. e.g. 1
pattern

At the video cycle, identify the stationary marker grid and write the complete ordered list of demonstrated visited nodes, including the initial red node. Encode nodes as [row,column], using zero-based rows top to bottom and columns left to right in the front image. Follow the stick and changes in red endpoints and connecting traces chronologically. Do not add duplicates for repeated frames at one endpoint; do include genuine revisits and intermediate visited endpoints along collinear segments. During every act cycle copy the incoming list unchanged. e.g. [[2,1],[2,2],[1,2],[0,1]]
reached_index

Write 0 during the video cycle and at execution step zero: the stick starts on pattern[0]. At later act cycles, start a working index at incoming reached_index and scan the motion frames chronologically, using the current wrist image and TCP pose as additional evidence. Whenever arrival at pattern[working index + 1] is established by stick position within 1 cm and supporting endpoint activation, increment the working index and continue checking for arrival at its successor. Confirm every consecutive arrival shown, without a one-increment-per-cycle limit. Write the final working index. Proximity outside 1 cm, an action-only near-arrival allowance, or choosing an onward waypoint does not advance this field. If no steps executed, retain the incoming value. e.g. 1
inst.subgoal:
During the video cycle write memory only. Execution starts with the stick already at the first demonstrated node; do not command that starting pose again. Identify the square marker grid from the current front image, using the wrist image to resolve occlusion. Its spacing is 0.10 m and its center is (x,y)=(-0.10,0). For an N-by-N grid, node [r,c] has x=-0.10+0.10*(r-(N-1)/2) and y=0.10*(c-(N-1)/2). Thus upward in the front image means decreasing world x, and rightward means increasing world y. Count actual grid rows and columns, not just currently unobscured markers. Use calibration and visible markers to check this registration.

Compute the latest strictly confirmed index by applying the memory update rule to all this cycle's motion frames, confirming every consecutive arrival shown without a one-arrival limit. Normally select the node immediately after that index. If steps have executed, the current TCP is within 0.012 m of that node's ideal waypoint, and the observed motion is consistent with finishing the segment to it, treat that one node as complete for action selection and select its successor instead. This allowance does not change reached_index, does not apply recursively, and cannot skip any other unconfirmed node. If a target remains, command exactly its ideal world x and y, z=0.070 m, retaining the current approximately downward TCP orientation. Keep the gripper closed (command -1; the stick interface ignores it). Move directly between successive demonstrated endpoints, including diagonals, without lifting, adding intermediate waypoints, or pausing to reproduce demonstration timing. Target the ideal grid coordinates rather than adding an offset to the imperfect current TCP pose. Strictly confirmed arrival or the action-only near-arrival case above is sufficient to move on; do not correct residual errors covered by these conditions.

Retry the next unconfirmed endpoint only when neither strict confirmation nor the action-only near-arrival case applies. If a motion executed no steps, do not advance progress; re-estimate the endpoint from the available images and retry a reachable, nonidentical waypoint toward it. If registration is uncertain, fit the regular 0.10 m grid to visible markers using calibration and the known current stick node, then use the best-supported next endpoint from pattern; do not invent a different pattern. Once the final endpoint is strictly confirmed or satisfies the action-only near-arrival case, make no additional tracing motion; if another response is required before automatic termination, wait a single control step to allow success evaluation.

RouteStick.label: Initial
fields: demonstration

At the video cycle, record the ordered list of all supplied demonstration frame labels, including the initial and final frames. Preserve this list unchanged throughout execution. These images specify the entire demonstrated route, including obstacle sides, intermediate turns, reversals, repeated visits and the stopping point; do not replace it with an unordered set of visited places. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V99"]
completed_legs

The number of demonstrated waypoint-to-waypoint legs already completed by the execution at the current observation, excluding the action selected at this cycle. Set to zero at the video cycle and the initial act cycle. Increment when the observed execution reaches the next demonstrated leg endpoint within 1 cm. Count intermediate bypass points as endpoints, not just marked gaps. Repeated visits count separately in chronological order. Do not increment for a motion that executes no steps, an incomplete approach, or a wait. Preserve the count otherwise. e.g. 2

completed_legs

Write zero at the video cycle and initial act cycle. At subsequent act cycles, use the incoming count to identify the next uncompleted endpoint in demonstration. Compare the current TCP and the observed motion with that endpoint. Increment by one only if the motion shown has reached it within 1 cm; otherwise preserve the count. Count bypass endpoints and repeated visits separately. An explicitly zero-step action, an incomplete approach or a wait does not advance the count. Record only arrivals already observed, never the endpoint of the action being selected now. e.g. 2
inst.subgoal:
At the video cycle, produce memory only. At execution start, the stick is already at the demonstrated starting point: do not add a grasp, lift or approach action. Use demonstration to reconstruct the ordered planar route of the lower free end of the attached stick. Follow the actual stick tip, not the robot housing or the red marker: a red marker can remain at the previous gap while the tip travels around an obstacle. The white trail helps identify which side was traversed, but is not itself the complete task history.

Infer the route's leg endpoints from successive changes of travel direction, including bypass points beside the ends of obstacles and arrivals at gaps. In these demonstrations a leg lasts approximately 25 control steps; useful endpoint times are approximately 0, 25, 50 and so on through the final frame. The frames straddle these times, so reconstruct the turning point from the adjacent incoming and outgoing trajectories rather than treating every displayed frame as a waypoint. Use the full video to distinguish retracing a bypass from continuing around the opposite end. Preserve all repetitions: reaching a previously visited gap does not mean the route is finished. Do not assume that all obstacles must be visited or that every traversal alternates sides.

Recover endpoint positions geometrically using the camera calibration and the tip's plane z=0.07 m. Intersect the ray through the lower free end with that plane; do not intersect the robot hand or upper end of the stick. When the tip is partially occluded, use neighboring demonstration frames, the visible shaft, obstacle geometry and the incoming/outgoing path to infer its endpoint. Ground-level marker centers must be reconstructed on their own ground plane rather than being treated as tip-height pixels. Use current front and wrist observations to refine alignment with the same static obstacle arrangement. Colors identify obstacles within the episode but do not define a universal route.

First evaluate whether the current observation completes the next leg, according to the completed_legs memory rule. With the resulting completed count c, command the endpoint of leg c+1. Set TCP z to 0.07 m and preserve the current approximately downward orientation, normalizing equivalent roll angles if needed. Keep the gripper closed; its command is ignored for this stick tool. Command the demonstrated full leg endpoint, typically about 12 cm away, rather than inserting arbitrary small subdivisions, lifting over an obstacle, or moving directly across an obstacle to a later gap. Accept normal arrival error within 1 cm and move on instead of issuing a redundant correction to a reached endpoint.

If the expected endpoint has not been reached, retain the count and complete that leg. If localization is ambiguous, use the retained video's neighboring frames and the current wrist view to select the endpoint consistent with both route order and obstacle clearance; never choose a later occurrence merely because it is closer. If a direct recovery would intersect an obstacle, make a conservative planar correction toward the demonstrated safe corridor without advancing the count until its endpoint is reached. Do not issue an identical-pose motion. If all demonstrated legs are complete and the environment has not yet terminated, hold with a short wait solely to allow terminal evaluation; do not start an extra loop.

Identify the ordered legs and assign demonstration frames to their incoming and outgoing segments, including bypasses beside obstacle ends and arrivals at gaps. Approximate 25-control-step boundaries are segmentation aids only: a nearby displayed frame need not show an endpoint, and elapsed time must not be converted into distance by assuming constant speed. Reconstruct unsampled endpoints geometrically as described below. Use the full video to distinguish retracing a bypass from continuing around the opposite end. Preserve all repetitions as separate chronological occurrences; reaching a previously visited gap does not mean the route is finished. Do not force bypass turns on opposite-direction traversals to share coordinates merely because they pass the same obstacle end. For each usable demonstration frame, locate the lower free end of the stick, not the upper shaft, robot housing, marker or trail. Convert its pixel (u,v) into world coordinates using the camera calibration: C=-R^T t, d=R^T K^-1[u,v,1]^T, and X=C+((0.07-C_z)/d_z)d. Perform this ray-plane calculation rather than estimating metric offsets visually.

For an unsampled turn, fit the incoming and outgoing planar path directions from tip positions on their respective legs, using multiple frames wherever available. Extend those fitted segments to their intersection to recover the shared endpoint; with noisy observations, use a joint least-squares fit with a shared endpoint. Do not interpolate directly between the last incoming sample and first outgoing sample, which cuts across the corner. Those two samples alone do not determine two directions: use neighboring frames farther along each segment, clearly observed start or arrival positions, and obstacle geometry as additional constraints. For collinear reversals, where line intersection does not determine the endpoint, use observed arrival or repeated-visit evidence and gap geometry rather than inventing an intersection. Project the recovered endpoint back into the demonstration to check consistency with both segments and the demonstrated obstacle side. When the tip is occluded, use neighboring visible tip positions, shaft and trail evidence, and obstacle geometry as supporting constraints; do not substitute shaft or trail pixels into the tip-height projection.

For a gap arrival, distinguish the full arrival from a sample still approaching the gap. Locate the endpoint from incoming and outgoing path evidence, refining it with the marked gap center only when the marker's own plane is established. Recover the marker's planar coordinates on that plane, then set the commanded TCP height to 0.07 m; never project a ground-marker pixel onto the tip-height plane. The retained starting view or a clearly observed visit to the same gap can supply an additional localization constraint without merging separate route occurrences. For the final endpoint, prioritize the actual lower tip in the final demonstration frame, corroborated by preceding arrival frames, and project it onto z=0.07 m. Do not extrapolate beyond it to a nominal gap coordinate or nominal leg length.

Use current front and wrist observations to refine alignment with the same static obstacle arrangement. Colors identify obstacles within the episode but do not define a universal route.

Neither a nominal leg length nor a fixed axial or diagonal offset defines that endpoint. Do not insert arbitrary small subdivisions, lift over an obstacle, or move directly across an obstacle to a later gap.
